[[File:John OSBORN (Strasbourg).png|thumb|John Osborn]]
'''John A. Osborn''' (1939–2000) was an [[inorganic chemist]] who made contributions to [[organometallic chemistry]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schrock, R.|year=2001|title=In Memory of John Anthony Osborn|journal=Adv. Synth. Catal.|volume=343|pages=3–4|doi=10.1002/1615-4169(20010129)343:1<3::AID-ADSC3>3.0.CO;2-Q}}</ref>  During that degree Osborn contributed to the development of [[Wilkinson's catalyst]].

== Education ==
He studied at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]], receiving a bachelor's degree with honors. In 1962, he obtained a PhD from [[Imperial College London]] under the supervision of Sir [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]] ([[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]], 1973). During this period, he contributed to the development of Wilkinson's catalyst RhCl(PPh<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.<ref name="Osborn">{{cite journal|last1=Osborn |first1=J. A. |last2=Jardine|first2=F. H. |last3=Young |first3=J. F. |last4=Wilkinson |first4=G.|author4-link=Geoffrey Wilkinson| title=The Preparation and Properties of Tris(triphenylphosphine)halogenorhodium(I) and Some Reactions Thereof Including Catalytic Homogeneous Hydrogenation of Olefins and Acetylenes and Their Derivatives| journal= [[Journal of the Chemical Society A|J. Chem. Soc. A]] | year = 1966|volume=1966 | pages = 1711–1732 | doi = 10.1039/J19660001711}}</ref>  His thesis studies ranged widely.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Thomas, K. |author2=Osborn, J. A. |author3=Powell, A. R. |author4=Wilkinson, G. |title=Preparation of Hydridopentammine- and Hydridoaquotetramminerhodium(III) Sulfates and Other Salts; the Formation of Alkyl and Fluoroalkyl derivatives|journal=J. Chem. Soc. A|year=1968|pages=1801–1806|doi=10.1039/j19680001801}}</ref>

== Career ==
Osborn's first independent position was at [[Harvard University|Harvard]]. His first doctoral student was [[Richard R. Schrock]] (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2005), followed by John R. Shapley and Jay A. Labinger. During this time, the chemistry of [M(diene)(PR<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> was advanced (M = Rh, Ir), laying the foundation for many subsequent developments.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Osborn, J. A. |author2=Schrock, R. R. |year=1971 |title=Coordinatively unsaturated cationic complexes of rhodium(I), iridium(I), palladium(II), and platinum(II). Generation, synthetic utility, and some catalytic studies |journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc. |volume=93 |issue=12 |pages=3089–3091 |doi=10.1021/ja00741a069}}</ref>  With Schrock, he developed the Schrock-Osborn catalyst [(PR<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>RhS<sub>2</sub>]+ (S = solvent), which is a cationic species derived from the Wilkinson catalyst.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schrock |first=Richard R. |last2=Osborn |first2=John A. |date=1976 |title=Catalytic hydrogenation using cationic rhodium complexes. I. Evolution of the catalytic system and the hydrogenation of olefins |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00424a020 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=98 |issue=8 |pages=2134–2143 |doi=10.1021/ja00424a020 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schrock |first=Richard R. |last2=Osborn |first2=John A. |date=1976 |title=Catalytic hydrogenation using cationic rhodium complexes. II. The selective hydrogenation of alkynes to cis olefins |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00424a021 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=98 |issue=8 |pages=2143–2147 |doi=10.1021/ja00424a021 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

At Harvard, he taught [[organometallic chemistry]] and [[homogeneous catalysis]] with transition metals, inspiring many students to pursue careers in this field, including [[Ryōji Noyori]] (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2001), who was a postdoctoral student at Harvard at the same time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ryoji Noyori – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2001/noyori/biographical/ |access-date=2025-08-16 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> He met [[Jean-Marie Lehn]] (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1987), who was a visiting professor at Harvard in 1972 and then in 1974, and who invited him to join the [[Louis Pasteur University]] of Strasbourg in 1975.

In Strasbourg, he became a university professor and headed a CNRS-university research laboratory until his untimely death. During this period, he developed:

- tungsten(VI)-based [[olefin metathesis]] catalysts, known to be extremely active;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kress |first=Jacky |last2=Osborn |first2=John A. |date=1983 |title=Tungsten carbene complexes in olefin metathesis: a cationic and chiral active species |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00358a044 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=105 |issue=20 |pages=6346–6347 |doi=10.1021/ja00358a044 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

- catalytic systems for [[carbonylation]] reactions (palladium-based)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Huser |first=Marc |last2=Youinou |first2=Marie‐ Thérèse |last3=Osborn |first3=John A. |date=1989 |title=Chlorocarbon Activation: Catalytic Carbonylation of Dichloromethane and Chlorobenzene |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.198913861 |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English |language=en |volume=28 |issue=10 |pages=1386–1388 |doi=10.1002/anie.198913861 |issn=0570-0833|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[hydrosilylation]] reactions (platinum-based);<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Steffanut |first=Pascal |last2=Osborn |first2=John A. |last3=DeCian |first3=Andre |last4=Fisher |first4=Jean |date=1998-10-02 |title=Efficient Homogeneous Hydrosilylation of Olefins by Use of Complexes of Pt0 with Selected Electron-Deficient Olefins as Ligands |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1521-3765(19981002)4:103.0.CO;2-K |journal=Chemistry - A European Journal |language=en |volume=4 |issue=10 |pages=2008–2017 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1521-3765(19981002)4:10<2008::AID-CHEM2008>3.0.CO;2-K |issn=0947-6539|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

- the asymmetric synthesis of amines by hydrogenation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ng Cheong Chan |first=Y. |last2=Osborn |first2=J. A. |date=1990 |title=Iridium(III) hydride complexes for the catalytic enantioselective hydrogenation of imines |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00181a056 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=112 |issue=25 |pages=9400–9401 |doi=10.1021/ja00181a056 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

- the catalytic properties of oxo (M=O) and imido (M=NR) complexes leading to new rhenium(VII) molecular catalysts for the rearrangement of allylic alcohols.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bellemin‐Laponnaz |first=Stéphane |last2=Gisie |first2=Hervé |last3=Le Ny |first3=Jean Pierre |last4=Osborn |first4=John A. |date=1997-05-16 |title=Mechanistic Insights into the Very Efficient [ReO3OSiR3]‐Catalyzed Isomerization of Allyl Alcohols |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.199709761 |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English |language=en |volume=36 |issue=9 |pages=976–978 |doi=10.1002/anie.199709761 |issn=0570-0833|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
